section_1.title: Introduction & Prerequisites (1 minute)
section_1.content: Briefly review the area of a circle (πr²) and the concept of a sphere. Establish the 'Parallel Light Assumption'—where light rays travel in straight, parallel lines to create a perfect circular shadow of a sphere.
section_1.example: An orange held under a bright, distant desk lamp projecting a crisp shadow on a table.

section_2.title: Conceptualizing the Sphere Surface (1.5 minutes)
section_2.content: Introduce the formula for the surface area of a sphere (A = 4πr²). Visualize this by 'unwrapping' the sphere. Use an animation showing four identical flat circles (each πr²) being mapped onto the curved surface of the sphere to demonstrate why the total area equals 4πr².
section_2.example: Imagine a hollow sphere made of play-dough; if we flatten its surface, it perfectly covers exactly four circles of the same radius as the sphere.

section_3.title: The Projection Logic (1.5 minutes)
section_3.content: Compare the 3D surface area (4πr²) to the 2D projected shadow area (πr²). Highlight that the shadow captures only the cross-section. Use an animation of a sphere spinning; note that regardless of rotation, the shadow remains a circle of area πr².
section_3.example: A robotic probe in space detecting a planet. The sensor 'sees' only the circular shadow (πr²), while the actual surface area it must traverse is four times larger (4πr²).

section_4.title: Summary & Application (1 minute)
section_4.content: Synthesize the 4:1 ratio. Emphasize that the sphere's surface is 4 times the area of its shadow. Conclude with the importance of this factor in light absorption (solar panels on spheres) or heat radiation.
section_4.example: Calculations for a spherical heat-shielding satellite: Understanding that to protect the whole surface, one must account for 4x the energy intercepted by its cross-sectional shadow.

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):

        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
